catalog_quote: 5.3.1 Stress: there is one degree of phonemic stress, /'/, which occurs on the first or second syllable of 2 or 3 syllable * words; and on the first, second, or third of 4 syllable words. 5.3.2 The following contrasts have been found:- /'faga/ ('faga) 'pretence' /fa'ga/ (fa'ga) 'root vegetable' /'aƀi/ ('aƀi) 'yam (general name)' /a'ƀi/ 'a'ƀi) 'a white sweet-potato' /se'gitaƀe/ (se'gitaƀe) 'a flower' /segi'taƀe/ (segi'taƀe) 'centipede' /me'tepuhi/ (me'tepuhi) 'darkness' /mete'puhi/ (mete'puhi) 'a yellow sweet potato' /'yago/ ('yago) 'yesterday/tomorrow' /ya'go/ (ya'go) 'its a fact (medial form)' /'kafe/ ('kafe) 'door' /ka'fa/ (ka'fa) 'rat' * Note: This analysis was based on nouns of up to 4 syllables. [p.18] /'akepa/ ('akepa) 'wild cane' /a'gepa/ (a'gepa) 'fern parsely' ... /'kese?i/ ('kese?i) 'a sugar cane' /ke'su?i/ (ke'su?i) 'tapioca' 5.3.3 A non-phonemic, secondary stress occurs in words of more than 3 syllables and is always two syllables removed from the primary stress placement. Examples of secondary stress, ("), are:- /'hetofana/ ('heto"fana) 'good' ... /segi'taƀe/ ("segi'taƀe) 'centipede' ... /'imima?i/ ('imi"ma?i) 'earthquake' 5.3.4 A shift of stress: a change of stress placement has been observed in some instances. However, since this always occurs in conjunction with morphological or intonational changes, it has not been included in this statement. The words on which the foregoing analysis is based are simple un-inflected nouns.

Sec. 5.3 'Supra-segmental Items' is exactly where stated. 5.3.1 reads verbatim: 'Stress: there is one degree of phonemic stress, /'/, which occurs on the first or second syllable of 2 or 3 syllable * words; and on the first, second, or third of 4 syllable words.' with footnote '* Note: This analysis was based on nouns of up to 4 syllables.' 5.3.2 lists the stress-only pairs /'faga/ ('faga) 'pretence' vs /fa'ga/ (fa'ga) 'root vegetable', /'abi/ 'yam' vs /a'bi/ 'a white sweet-potato', /se'gitabe/ 'a flower' vs /segi'tabe/ 'centipede', /m…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive): a single primary stress may fall on the 1st or 2nd syllable of di- and trisyllabic nouns and on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable of quadrisyllabic nouns, with minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone; it is never reported on the final syllable of 3-4-syllable words. Confirmed by the 1992/2004 SIL OPD ('Stress is phonemic, but is not written') and Young 1975 ('Stress, phonemically distinguishable, is not marked').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-phonemic secondary stress in words of more than three syllables, always two syllables away from the primary (e.g. 'heto"fana 'good', "segi'tabe 'centipede', 'imi"ma?i 'earthquake'), i.e. an alternating rhythm anchored on the lexical primary.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts under inflection and intonation were observed but excluded; the analysis covers only simple uninflected nouns of up to 4 syllables (words run to 8 syllables). Sec. 8.1: when adjacent syllables have identical vowels and stress is on the second, the first (unstressed) vowel is extremely short.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms of uninflected nouns; the word is defined (6.1.2) as the unit bearing exactly one primary stress; the syllable (6.1.1) is 'a unit of actual or potential stress placement'.
new_statements.identity_note: Young & Young 1961 describe Bena-bena as spoken just east of Goroka (SIL work based at Segeya per the 1992 OPD); language-level bena1264, no sub-dialect singled out. The 1961 stress analysis is explicitly restricted to simple uninflected nouns of up to 4 syllables.

new_statements.quote: In KAMANO and BENABENA it is a phoneme of stress which contrasts with syllables which are unstressed. [...] BENABENA fa'ga "a root vegetable" / 'faga "pretence" / se'gitabe "balsam" / segi'tabe "centipede" / me'tepuhi "darkness" / mete'puhi "a yellow sweet-potato" [...] In BENABENA there are two degrees of intensity of stress, the lighter stress being predictable in terms of the heavier, so that the stress phoneme has two allophones (heavy) and (light). Light stress occurs in words of more than three syllables and is two syllables removed from the heavy stress. So, if heavy stress is on the first syllable, light stress is on the third and vice versa.

Light stress occurs in words of more than three syllables and is two syllables removed from the heavy stress. So, if heavy st…
new_statements.relation_note: Same analysis as the catalog's existing Young & Young 1961 statement (contrastive, lexically placed stress with the same minimal pairs) and adds the secondary-stress rule stated as 'two degrees of intensity' with the light stress an allophone of the heavy one. It compares Benabena explicitly with Kamano (also stress, but one degree and up to two stresses per word) and with Kanite and Gahuku (tone, not stress).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Benabena has one contrastive suprasegmental phoneme, a stress, which distinguishes words that are segmentally identical (fa'ga vs 'faga, se'gitabe vs segi'tabe, me'tepuhi vs mete'puhi): its position is not predictable from the segmental string. There are two degrees of intensity; the heavy stress is the phoneme, the light stress is its predictable allophone, appearing in words of more than three syllables two syllables away from the heavy stress (heavy on 1 -> light on 3, and vice versa).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: a predictable 'light' stress (allophone of the stress phoneme) in words of more than three syllables, always two syllables removed from the heavy stress; p. 99.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Benabena; p. 94 adds that /y/ is realised [y] (semivowel) initially in stressed syllables and [z] in unstressed syllables, i.e. stress conditions consonant allophony. The excerpt on archive.org covers only pp. 93-99 of the article; pp. 100-110 were not seen (SIL record 3292 says the article is 'Not Available Online').
new_statements.identity_note: All opened works describe Bena-bena (Benabena, ISO bef) of the Goroka area, Eastern Highlands, as analysed by Robert and Rosemary Young (SIL). Young 1975 states that dialect variation is minimal (one small dialect around Kenemalo, Megabo and Pumalihi lacks the /b/-/m/ contrast; the Dunantina-valley border with Kamano adds a glottal stop before nasals) and mentions no dialect difference in stress. Young 1962 treats Benabena beside Kamano (stress, one degree, up to two stresses per word, final syllable never stressed), Kanite and Gahuku (tone); those statements are about the other three languages, not Bena-bena. The 1961 stress analysis is based on simple uninflected nouns of up to four syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One phonemic (contrastive) stress per word whose position is not predictable: on the first or second syllable of 2- and 3-syllable words, on the first, second or third of 4-syllable words, with minimal pairs. A non-phonemic secondary stress falls two syllables from the primary in words of more than three syllables. The analysis is based on simple uninflected nouns of up to four syllables; stress shifts under morphological or intonational change are noted but excluded.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, non-phonemic, always two syllables from the primary stress in words of more than three syllables, e.g. ('heto"fana) 'good', ("segi'tabe) 'centipede', ('imi"ma?i) 'earthquake'; sec. 5.3.3 p. 18.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 5.3.4 p. 18: stress placement shifts under morphological or intonational change (excluded from the statement); footnote p. 17: analysis based on nouns of up to 4 syllables. Sec. 5.3.5 p. 18-19: stress, pitch, pause and vowel length are components of intonation patterning, not analysed.

new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Rendered p. 2 (printed p. 1, 'Notes on the Dialect Differences of Bena-bena, Aug. 1975, Young, SIL'). The first sentence is as quoted. The stress line on the page scan (300 dpi crop) reads 'Stress, phemically distinguishable, is not marked.' -- the typescript itself has the typo 'phemically'; the compiler claim that the page scan reads 'phonemically' is wrong, the scanned was faithful. Substance unchanged: stress is phonemic (contrastive) and unwritten; no placement rule, nothing on dialect differences in stress. Reading lexical (unpredictable) is an inference from 'phonemically distinguishable' only, so it is thin but consistent; relation 'agrees' is right.
new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the phonemic (contrastive) status of stress recorded from Young & Young 1961; adds no placement information. Note the scanned file reads 'phemically' where the page scan reads 'phonemically'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Only says that stress is phonemically distinctive and is left unwritten in the practical orthography; no placement rule. The rest of the note (pp. 1-3) covers a /b/~/m/ merger in one small dialect, glottal stop before nasals in the Dunantina valley border area, and vocabulary preferences; it says nothing about dialect differences in stress.
